title: Caro-Kann plans
summary: In the Caro-Kann and the Slav, bring out the light-squared bishop before ...e6. Then break the centre with ...c5.
body:
### One plan for two openings

The Caro-Kann and the Slav have the same shape. Black plays ...c6 and ...d5. This gives a solid pawn centre. But it also gives one problem: the light-squared bishop on c8.

If you play ...e6 first, your bishop stays behind your own pawns. It does nothing for a long time. So use this order:

- **Bishop first.** Play the bishop outside the pawn chain, usually to f5. In the Caro-Kann you play it after White plays e5, or after White takes on e4. In the Slav you play it before ...e6.
- **Then ...e6.** This pawn guards your bishop and your centre.
- **Knights and the other bishop.** Play ...Nf6 (or ...Ne7 in the Advance). Put the second knight on d7 or e7. Put the dark-squared bishop on e7 or d6. Then castle.
- **Break with ...c5.** This pawn attacks White's d4 pawn. It is the main plan in both openings. In some Slav lines you can also play ...e5.

Watch your bishop on f5. White can attack it with a knight, or with the g-pawn. Keep a piece nearby that guards it. In the Advance Caro-Kann, the knight on e7 does this job.

Do not rush ...c5 before your bishop is out. The Semi-Slav is an exception: with ...dxc4 and ...b5, the bishop goes to b7 later and ...c5 comes first.

The exercises use positions from your repertoire. Find the idea in each one: bishop out, knight to guard, pawn break.

Rule of thumb: bishop out before ...e6, then break with ...c5.

exercises.prompt: Black to move. Develop your light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain.
exercises.explanation: Bf5 puts the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 closes it in. After ...e6 first, the bishop stays stuck behind its own pawns.

exercises.prompt: Black to move. Develop your light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain.
exercises.explanation: In the Slav you play the bishop before ...e6. Bf5 is the plan. Bg4 is also fine, but it is not our plan. After ...e6 first, the bishop is shut in.

exercises.prompt: Black to move. Attack White's centre with a pawn.
exercises.explanation: The bishop is out, ...e6 is played and a knight can follow. Now ...c5 attacks the d4 pawn. A waiting move such as ...a6 does nothing against White's centre.

exercises.prompt: Black to move. Develop a knight and protect your bishop.
exercises.explanation: The white knight on d4 attacks your bishop on f5. Ne7 guards it. After ...Nc6, Nxf5 exf5 breaks your pawns.

exercises.prompt: Black to move. Break up White's centre with a pawn.
exercises.explanation: White has built a big centre. ...c5 hits the d4 pawn and fights for the centre. If you wait, White plays e5 and gets more space.

exercises.prompt: Black to move. Bring out your dark-squared bishop.
exercises.explanation: The bishop must leave f8 so you can castle. Bd6 looks at White's kingside and prepares ...e5. Be7 is safer but more passive.
